input.headline: G7 industry and digital ministers, meeting in Canada, issue joint declaration on AI, quantum and supply chains, plus a plan to help small firms adopt AI.

input_full.excerpt: The G7 Industry, Digital and Technology Ministers’ Meeting 2025, held in Montréal under Canada’s G7 presidency, brought together ministers to advance cooperation on AI, quantum technologies, digital policy and industrial resilience. The meeting produced a set of headline political and technical deliverables that structure the G7’s digital–industry agenda for the coming period. The core political outcome was the G7 2025 Industry, Digital and Technology Ministerial Declaration, which set out shared commitments on: (1) using AI for inclusive economic growth; (2) developing quantum technologies; (3) strengthening a resilient and competitive digital economy; and (4) reinforcing secure and resilient industrial and digital supply chains. A second major outcome was the G7 Industry, Digital and Technology Ministerial Statement on the SME AI Adoption Blueprint. The statement translated the leaders’ “AI for Prosperity” direction into a targeted agenda for helping small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) adopt AI safely and effectively while respecting competition, data protection and intellectual property frameworks. Linked to that statement, the SME AI Adoption Blueprint itself was issued as a practical, more technical deliverable. It offers concrete guidance, policy options, examples and support measures that G7 governments can use to lower barriers and scale responsible AI uptake by SMEs across their economies.

input.headline: Brazil bill proposes national AI governance system: new advisory council, data protection authority as residual AI regulator, expert committees, high-risk use criteria.

input_full.excerpt: The Law would establish a regulatory framework for AI called the National System for the Development, Regulation, and Governance of AI (SIA), composed of a newly established Brazilian Council for Artificial Intelligence (CBIA), the Brazilian Data Protection Authority (ANPD), two newly established committees composed of experts and civil society representatives, and other related public bodies. The CBIA would be responsible for establishing guidelines and principles for AI in relation to economic development, digital sovereignty, and social inclusion, advising the President of the Republic on AI policy development, and coordinating with other authorities on sectoral issues. The ANPD would become the residual regulator and supervising authority for AI, with the power to issue binding rules, including regarding incident reporting and algorithmic impact assessments, request clarification on data used to train high-risk AI in the public sector, and publish a list of high-risk AI use cases. Further, the Law would require the ANPD and sectoral agencies to define new categories for high-risk AI, based on criteria such as impact on fundamental rights, vulnerable groups, risk of systemic cybersecurity harm, and impact on the development of children and adolescents. The statement of reasons notes that Congress is already examining Bill 2338/2023, and the Executive must be prepared to implement whichever regulatory model is adopted. The Law therefore organises Brazil’s AI governance by assigning responsibilities to the CBIA, ANPD, expert and civil-society committees, and sectoral regulators to support coordinated oversight.

input.headline: G7 leaders issue joint summit statement endorsing shared principles for children's online safety, urging default safeguards on conversational AI tools and age assurance for minors.

input_full.excerpt: The G7 heads of state and government, comprising the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, and Japan, along with the President of the European Council and the President of the European Commission, issued joint statements at the 52nd G7 Summit in Évian-les-Bains, France. The statements include commitments relevant to AI governance, emphasizing the development and application of AI systems that ensure safe, secure, and age-appropriate digital experiences for minors, with a focus on online safety for children and youth under 18. Among other matters, the G7: (1) recognizes the opportunities and risks associated with conversational AI tools, emphasizing the need for safety settings by default, including parental controls and age assurance solutions, to protect children and youth, and supports industry efforts to improve transparency regarding content provenance, digital literacy, and awareness; (2) reaffirms its commitment to prohibiting the generation, manipulation, and distribution of child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes involving minors, online grooming, sexual exploitation, and extortion, requiring digital service providers to implement effective detection and removal measures, with particular attention to harms disproportionately affecting girls, young women, boys, and young men; (3) advocates sharing best practices, fostering research, and developing a scientific ecosystem to study the benefits and challenges of digital and AI technologies, emphasizing transparency, accountability, and the importance of data sharing, impartial evaluations, and common assessment standards to evaluate AI models’ impact on minors’ safety; and (4) endorses the G7 Common Set of Principles for a safer digital environment for minors, commits to regular meetings to assess progress, and highlights the importance of ongoing dialogue with partner countries to ensure the effective implementation of these measures by the end of the year.

input.headline: Australian junior digital economy minister urges domestic AI industry, renewable-powered data centres, warning foreign platforms could capture AI profits; targets billions in annual revenue.

input_full.excerpt: In a speech to the Australian Business Economics conference, Assistant Technology and Digital Economy Minister Andrew Charlton cautioned against the "Uberisation" of the Australian economy, a trajectory in which the nation merely rents foreign digital platforms and allows the resulting profits to flow offshore. Characterizing AI as a critical general-purpose technology akin to electrification, the Minister argued that while AI will inevitably reorganize global production, the domestic distribution of its benefits depends entirely on ownership and market structure. Charlton emphasized that without a strategic "pro-creation" approach, Australia risks a "productivity paradox" in which efficiency rises but national income stagnates as rents accrue to foreign capital. To mitigate this, the Minister proposed a comprehensive "AI stack" strategy that leverages Australia’s comparative advantage in renewable energy to underwrite a domestic data center industry, noting that the country receives 58 million petajoules of solar radiation annually. By targeting a 0.5% increase in global AI market share, the government aims to generate an additional $25 billion in annual revenue and secure high-value employment. Ultimately, the address serves as a call for urgent, values-driven policy to ensure that the transition to an AI-driven economy augments the Australian labor force and fosters a "Future Made in Australia" rather than entrenching global capital concentration.

Identifying AI as the defining currency of the future, Kendall argued that nations that master AI will lead in economic and military power. The Tech Secretary also stressed the importance of AI sovereignty, which for the UK means reducing dependencies while fostering innovation and collaboration with international partners. Kendall outlined the government's initiatives, including the launch of Sovereign AI, which aims to invest £500 million in British AI companies and enhance the nation's AI hardware capabilities, as well as reinforced partnerships with countries such as Germany, Canada, and Japan. In conclusion, the Tech Secretary asserted that the UK must actively shape its AI future to ensure national interests are prioritized, advocating a proactive approach rather than retreating from technological progress.

input.headline: EU and Canada adopt summit joint statement forming new partnership, prioritising mutual recognition of AI conformity assessments, interoperable digital rules, shared supercomputing and AI cybersecurity cooperation.

input_full.excerpt: The European Union and Canada have adopted a joint statement at the 21st EU-Canada Summit, held in Montréal on 29–30 October 2026, establishing a Canada-EU Alliance for the Future. On AI, the parties commit to cooperate on AI security and safety, on the global governance of AI and sovereignty anchored in international law, and on free and trusted data flows and digital governance, with the stated aim of making AI models and systems and their respective digital regulatory frameworks interoperable. The statement provides for deeper joint work on advanced AI and high-performance computing capacity, including AI Factories, with attention to access for start-ups, small and medium-sized enterprises, researchers and public-sector users, and records Canada's participation in the European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking (EuroHPC JU) to further integrate the two AI innovation ecosystems. The statement identifies mutual recognition of conformity assessment results for AI systems as one of three priority digital areas, alongside digital identity, credentials and trust services, and cybersecurity. The parties also commit to expand cybersecurity cooperation with particular attention to AI-enabled threats, including automated cyberattacks, while promoting the responsible use of AI for threat detection and incident response. The statement further sets the objective of easing market access for each other's cloud and AI service and infrastructure providers, subject to each side's regulatory framework, and of aligning work on the online protection of children.

input.headline: Spain's data protection authority says it can already act against banned AI systems that process personal data, ahead of the EU's AI rules taking full effect.

input_full.excerpt: The Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) has issued guidance clarifying that it can already act against prohibited AI systems that process personal data before the EU AI Act is fully in force. From 2 August 2025, supervisory and sanctioning provisions under Article 5 of the AI Act, covering banned AI systems such as real-time biometric identification in public spaces, will begin to apply. Although Spain has not yet adopted its national AI law and the AEPD has not formally been designated as a market surveillance authority, the agency remains empowered to act in its capacity as data protection authority. This includes overseeing AI-driven data processing where it infringes data protection rights. The AEPD advises organisations using AI to begin preparing for AI Act compliance and is assessing the internal resources it needs to fulfil future responsibilities under the regulation.

input.headline: China proposes draft rules for AI services simulating human personalities, requiring providers to monitor users' emotions and dependence and intervene on addiction or extreme emotions.

input_full.excerpt: These measures aim to tighten oversight of AI services designed to simulate human personalities and engage users in emotional interaction. The proposed rules would apply to AI products and services offered to the public in China that present simulated human personality traits, thinking patterns and communication styles, and interact with users emotionally through text, images, audio, video or other means. The proposed measures would: (1) require service providers to assume safety responsibilities throughout the product lifecycle and establish systems for algorithm review, data security and personal information protection; (2) target potential psychological risks by requiring providers to identify user states and assess users' emotions and their level of dependence on the service; (3) require providers to take necessary measures to intervene if users are found to exhibit extreme emotions or addictive behaviour; and (4) set content and conduct red lines, stating that services must not generate content that endangers national security, spreads rumours or promotes violence or obscenity.

input.headline: Nigeria's information minister urges broadcasters to verify facts, avoid hate speech and counter AI-generated misinformation ahead of upcoming national elections, speaking at a broadcasters' conference.

input_full.excerpt: Speaking at the 3rd Annual National Conference of the Society of Nigerian Broadcasters in Bauchi, Nigeria, Information and National Orientation Minister Mohammed Idris called on broadcasters to uphold accuracy, fairness and professional ethics as Nigeria approaches the 2027 elections. Represented by Voice of Nigeria (VON) Director-General Jibrin Baba Ndace, the Minister said broadcasters should verify information, distinguish facts from allegations, opinions and unverified claims, and provide properly contextualised reporting while continuing to scrutinise government, political parties, candidates and public institutions. Idris warned that AI and social media make it easier to spread false and manipulated content, and urged broadcasters to avoid hate speech, ethnic or religious provocation, and deliberate circulation of false information during the electoral period while preserving space for legitimate debate and criticism. The Minister also called on the Society and broadcasters to strengthen professional training, election reporting, verification and measures against AI-generated misinformation. Idris cited Federal Government investment in broadcasting, including the Digital Switch Over platform and the modernisation of the Nigerian Television Authority (NTA), the Federal Radio Corporation of Nigeria (FRCN) and VON.

input.headline: South Korean lawmakers introduce bill to amend national AI law, splitting generative AI labelling duties between model developers (machine-readable marks) and deployers (user-visible notices).

input_full.excerpt: The National Assembly has introduced the Bill amending the AI Basic Act, which aims to differentiate disclosure requirements for generative AI results based on business role. Current law requires AI operators to indicate that generative AI or its results were generated by AI but does not distinguish between the responsibilities of businesses that develop AI models and those that deploy them, leading to ambiguities in fulfilling disclosure obligations. The Bill seeks to modify the current law, which mandates uniform transparency obligations for all AI operators to indicate when generative AI generates products, services, or results. It does so by establishing distinct standards for: (1) AI development businesses, namely those that develop and provide AI models, application programming interfaces (APIs), and generative engines; and (2) AI user businesses, namely those that utilize AI to deliver final products and services, including applications, platforms, and content services. Specifically, the Bill mandates that AI development businesses display generative AI results using machine-readable methods aligned with international technical standards, while AI user businesses must display results in a manner that users can clearly recognize.

input.headline: A UN cultural agency and an international economic body, with input from leading industrial nations, release a toolkit helping governments turn trustworthy AI principles into public-sector policies.

input_full.excerpt: The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) and the OECD, with contributions from the G7, have developed a toolkit for policymakers and public sector leaders to translate principles for safe, secure, and trustworthy AI into actionable policies. The key messages of the toolkit are to: (1) establish clear strategic objectives and action plans in line with expected benefits; (2) include the voices of users in shaping strategies and implementation; (3) overcome siloed structures in government for effective governance; (4) establish robust frameworks for the responsible use of AI; (5) improve the scalability and replicability of successful AI initiatives; (6) enable a more systematic use of AI in and by the public sector; and (7) adopt an incremental and experimental approach to the deployment and use of AI in and by the public sector.

input_full.excerpt: Nigeria’s Federal Ministry of Communications, Innovation and Digital Economy, led by Minister Dr. ‘Bosun Tijani, has directed relevant sector regulators to maintain the regulatory status quo and defer the enforcement of recently issued regulations concerning Internet platforms and online intermediaries. The directive applies specifically to the Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC), the National Information Technology Development Agency (NITDA), and the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC). It aims to preserve legal certainty, promote innovation, and protect investor confidence while the Ministry coordinates the development of a harmonized national policy and governance framework. To execute this alignment without diminishing the statutory mandates of the individual agencies, the Ministry is establishing a Joint Technical Coordination Committee to spearhead technical engagements and consult with industry stakeholders, academia, and civil society. The aim is to ensure a unified, predictable, and future-ready regulatory approach to cross-cutting digital economy issues such as AI, online safety, and data governance.

input.headline: Türkiye's competition watchdog opens sector inquiry into AI value chain, examining data and computing access, entry barriers, lock-in and self-preferencing by digital platforms.

input_full.excerpt: Türkiye's Competition Authority (Rekabet Kurumu) has launched a comprehensive sector inquiry into the AI ecosystem to evaluate the transformative effects of AI on market dynamics and identify emerging competitive risks. The inquiry focuses on the AI value chain, which relies on a strategic structure from infrastructure to applications, emphasizing the importance of access to data, computing capacity, technical expertise, and funding for market positioning. The general-purpose nature of AI models, trained on large datasets, poses risks such as increased barriers to entry and user lock-in, necessitating an examination of access conditions and ecosystem relationships. Additionally, the integration of AI with existing digital platforms raises concerns regarding anti-competitive practices such as self-preferencing and exclusion, impacting future competition and innovation. Recent merger and acquisition assessments highlight the critical nature of AI in market control, prompting the inquiry to analyze the relationships within the value chain and the influence of data and computing power on competition. The findings will guide policy-making and intervention strategies to maintain competitive structures in Türkiye's economy amid the evolving AI landscape.
input_full.headline: Competition Authority launches strategic sector inquiry on AI

input.headline: UK upper chamber backs, by a large majority, amendment to data bill requiring AI firms to disclose copyrighted material used in models; bill returns to lower chamber.

input_full.excerpt: The House of Lords has voted 272 to 125 in favour of approving an amendment to the Data (Use and Access) Bill that would require AI companies to reveal which copyrighted material is used in their models, despite opposition in the House of Commons. The bill will now return to the House of Commons, and if the government removes the amendment, it will set the scene for another confrontation in the House of Lords next week.

input.headline: Türkiye presidential decree renames national technology directorate to include AI and creates new public-sector AI directorate under presidency's cybersecurity body, setting data-center standards.

input_full.excerpt: Under Presidential Decree No. 191, published in the Official Gazette, Türkiye has expanded its AI governance by renaming the Directorate General of National Technology as the Directorate General of National Technology and Artificial Intelligence. The renamed directorate will develop policies to enhance data center and cloud computing infrastructure, set standards for data centers, and oversee certification processes. Additionally, a Public Artificial Intelligence Directorate General has been established under the Presidency's Cybersecurity Directorate to guide AI use across government institutions, align national legislation with international frameworks, and set data governance standards for digital government and public sector AI applications.

input.headline: Australia's online safety regulator registers industry code requiring certain internet services, including generative AI tools, to curb harmful content and protect children through age and content controls.

input_full.excerpt: The eSafety Commissioner has registered the Designated Internet Services Online Safety Code (Class 1C and Class 2 Material) under the Online Safety Act 2021. The Code outlines a risk-based framework for designated internet services (DIS) to manage harmful content, with a focus on protecting children. Among other things, it includes provisions for emerging technologies, including generative AI services, which must prevent restricted content generation and implement age or content controls.

input.headline: East Asian democracy and Gulf federation agree several cooperation memorandums at leaders' summit covering artificial intelligence, aerospace and nuclear energy, including joint work on a US-backed giant AI data campus.

input_full.excerpt: South Korea and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) have signed seven memorandums of understanding to expand cooperation in strategic sectors (including AI, aerospace and nuclear energy) during a summit between President Lee Jae Myung and UAE President Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan. Notably, South Korea has agreed to work with the UAE on the US-backed Stargate project to build a massive new AI data campus in the UAE. Earlier, in October 2025, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix signed initial agreements to supply memory chips for OpenAI's Stargate data centers.

India's telecom regulator adopts recommendations for a sandbox framework testing innovations like AI in digital communications, stressing network security, consumer protection, exemptions and exit strategy.

input_full.excerpt: The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI) adopted its recommendations for a regulatory sandbox framework aimed at supporting innovation in areas such as AI in the digital communication sector. input.headline: Nigeria's federal and state civil service commissions, closing their annual national council, resolve to digitise personnel administration and create new job cadres in response to the implications of artificial intelligence.

input_full.excerpt: Speaking at the 45th Annual National Council of Civil Service Commissions of the Federation in Asaba, Delta State, Prof. Paul Samani Ywai, Chairman of the Communiqué Committee, presented resolutions calling for institutional re-engineering, digital transformation and culture change across Federal and State Civil Service Commissions. The Council urged commissions to digitise personnel records and administrative processes, review schemes of service and create relevant cadres in response to emerging professional demands, generational changes and the implications of AI. The communiqué also called for practical guidelines balancing merit and national spread in recruitment and appointments, effective use of the Performance Management System in promotion exercises, and a safeguarded framework for accelerated promotion of exceptionally performing officers.

input.headline: G7 ministers agree to set up a high-level group on advanced AI safety, plan to share risk assessments and evaluation methods, and work toward common international standards.

input_full.excerpt: Speaking at the G7 ministerial meeting on AI safety, Adolfo Urso, Italy’s Minister of Enterprises and Made in Italy, called for shared responses and common standards to address the risks and opportunities of advanced AI systems. The meeting concluded with a decision to establish a High Level Group on AI safety and to hold another meeting soon. Ministers discussed sharing assessments of emerging risks, safety-evaluation methodologies and data, as well as advancing convergence on international standards and regulations based on shared principles.

input.headline: UK signals intelligence chief, giving inaugural annual lecture at wartime codebreaking site, urges businesses to boost cyber defences amid AI advances and Russia, China threats.

input_full.excerpt: Speaking at the first Annual Lecture at Bletchley Park, the Director of the UK's Government Communications Headquarters (GCHQ), Anne Keast-Butler, emphasised the historical significance of the site. The Director further emphasised the contributions of women in intelligence during World War II, particularly through the efforts of early leaders such as Alastair Denniston. The lecture addressed the current landscape of national security, highlighting the urgent need for collaboration among intelligence agencies, the importance of managing technological advancements, and the risks posed by adversaries such as Russia and China. Director Keast-Butler underscored the critical role of data and cybersecurity in safeguarding national interests, advocating immediate action from businesses to enhance cyber defenses. The speech also touched on the need for innovation in encryption and the significance of international partnerships, particularly within the Five Eyes alliance, to counter emerging threats. Ultimately, the Director called for collective vigilance and preparedness in the face of evolving challenges, reiterating the necessity of harnessing technology responsibly for national security.

input_named.headline: UK cyberspying chief warns of peace and war amid AI advancements

input_full.excerpt: A draft law (published by the Ministry of Communications and the Ministry of Justice) which requires distributors of messages on large social networks to mark messages that are automatically distributed through technological applications, including “bots”.

input.headline: EU member states adopt position on amending supercomputing joint undertaking rules to create AI gigafactories via public-private partnerships and add quantum pillar; Parliament next.

input_full.excerpt: The European Council has adopted a position on the proposal for a regulation amending Regulation (EU) 2021/1173 as regards a EuroHPC initiative for start-ups to boost European leadership in trustworthy AI. The amendment sets the framework for the activities of the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking (EuroHPC JU) and updates the EuroHPC JU governance structure. It aims to establish AI gigafactories in Europe, which will be supported through public-private partnerships, and to establish a quantum pillar in the activities of the EuroHPC JU. The amendment also outlines the framework for establishing and operating such gigafactories, as well as rules for funding and procurement, and allows unused EU funds to be redirected to the project. Finally, it introduces safeguards for the participation of third countries. As a next step, the European Parliament is expected to give its opinion on 17 December 2025, after which the regulation will be up for final adoption.
input_full.headline: EU Council approve EuroHPC initiative for start-ups to boost European leadership in trustworthy AI, proceeding to Parliament

input.headline: Turkey: Bill introduced in parliament to set AI rules, including liability for crimes committed through AI, rapid deepfake takedowns, emergency blocking powers and mandatory labelling of AI content.

input_full.excerpt: A bill establishing an AI legal framework in Türkiye has been introduced to the Grand National Assembly. The proposed legislation would clarify responsibilities for both users and developers of AI, defining AI systems by amending Law No. 5651 and regulating liability for crimes committed through AI by modifying Penal Code No. 5237. Other key features include: (1) mandating removal of AI-generated content violating personality rights, threatening public safety, or using deepfake technology within six hours via modifications to Law No. 5651; (2) granting the Information Technologies and Communication Authority (BTK) emergency access blocking power for AI content threatening public order or election security, with fines up to TRY 10 million (modifies Law No. 5809); (3) amending the Cybersecurity Law (modifying Law No. 7545) to require AI service providers to implement content verification mechanisms and algorithmic controls reducing hallucination risks, subject to possible penalties of TRY 5 million for failure to do so; and (4) mandating clear labelling of AI-generated content, (modifies Law No. 5651), with fines between TRY 500'000 and 5'000'000 for violations, with the possibility of content provider blocking for systematic and intentional violations.
input_full.headline: Bill no. 2/3358

input_named.headline: Bill no. 2/3358

input.headline: Nigeria's telecoms regulator brings internet conduct code into force, with grace period, setting child-protection, content takedown, data-breach notification and transparency duties for internet providers and platforms.

input_full.excerpt: Nigeria’s Internet Code of Practice, a regulatory framework issued by the Nigerian Communications Commission (NCC), has entered into force with a grace period. The Code sets obligations for internet access providers and online/digital communication platforms to promote a safer, more responsible internet while balancing access, privacy, child protection, and lawful expression. It requires providers to: (1) publish clear terms and community rules; (2) protect minors and vulnerable users through parental controls and content safeguards; (3) block or report unlawful content when notified; (4) comply with data protection and cybersecurity requirements; (5) notify affected users and regulators of data breaches within 48 hours; (6) avoid discriminatory treatment of lawful content; (7) disclose traffic management practices transparently; and (8) submit periodic compliance reports to the NCC. The 2026 version also includes content moderation and quality-of-service rules, with limited proactive monitoring duties but obligations to assist law enforcement and follow takedown procedures where the Commission determines content is unlawful.
input_full.headline: Internet Code of Practice enters into force, covering AI and emerging technologies

input_named.headline: Internet Code of Practice enters into force, covering AI and emerging technologies
